subject: body
title: Food's Journey
about: Follows a bite of food from the mouth, where teeth chew and saliva softens it, down the food tube to the stomach that mixes it into a thick soup, through the long small intestine that passes the good parts into the blood, to the large intestine that takes back water, and out as poop a day or two later; also tummy rumbles, the liver, fiber and water. Digestion is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are 1.NPA.1.1 (why drink water), 1.NPA.1.2 (foods and why we eat them) and Science LS.1.1.1 (living things need food). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud, so you can trace the trip on his tummy as you go.
tip: At a meal, have him chew one bite slowly and count the chews, then follow the swallow with a finger down to his stomach.

cards.q: A bite of apple starts a long trip through your body. Where does the trip begin?
cards.note: The trip runs from your mouth all the way through you. These cards follow the bite step by step.

cards.q: What do your teeth do to a crunchy bite of apple?
cards.note: Front teeth bite, back teeth grind. Small bits are easier for the rest of your body to handle.

cards.q: The watery spit in your mouth has a science name. What is it?
cards.note: Say suh-LIE-vuh. It makes food soft and slippery and starts breaking it down, and just thinking about lemons makes it flow!

cards.q: Why is it smart to chew your food well before you swallow?
cards.note: Small, soft bits are easier for the stomach to mix. Chewing slowly also lets you taste more.

cards.q: You swallow. Which tube carries the food from your mouth down to your stomach?
cards.note: Its grown-up name is the esophagus, say ee-SOF-uh-gus. Its muscles squeeze food down, so you could even swallow upside down.

cards.q: The food tube ends in a stretchy bag that mixes food with juices. What is the bag?
cards.note: The stomach is a muscle bag. It churns and squeezes food with juices for a few hours.

cards.q: After the stomach mixes and squeezes, what does the food look like?
cards.note: The stomach turns even a crunchy carrot into a thick, mushy soup, ready for the next stop.

cards.q: Your tummy rumbles and growls. What is making that sound?
cards.note: Squeezing muscles push air and juice around. It is loudest when the stomach is empty, so it often means lunch time.

cards.q: After the stomach, food moves into a long, curly tube. What is it called?
cards.note: Say in-TES-tin. It is small around but very long, three or four times as long as you are tall, folded up neatly inside you.

cards.q: The small intestine takes the good parts out of food. Where do those good parts go next?
cards.note: Energy and building blocks pass through the intestine wall into the blood, which delivers them everywhere.

cards.q: Which big organ beside your stomach makes a juice that helps break down fats?
cards.note: The liver also cleans your blood and stores energy. The pancreas nearby makes more digesting juices.

cards.q: The last stop is the large intestine. What does it take back from what is left?
cards.note: The large intestine is wider but shorter. It soaks up water so your body can use it again.

cards.q: What is left leaves your body when you use the toilet. What is it called?
cards.note: Poop is the part of food your body could not use, and everyone makes it. Wash your hands after.

cards.q: About how long does food's whole trip through your body take?
cards.note: A day or two, sometimes three. The stomach part alone takes a few hours.

cards.q: Fruits, vegetables and whole grains have fiber. What does fiber do inside you?
cards.note: Fiber is the part of plants you cannot digest. It sweeps through the intestines and keeps things moving along.

cards.q: Which drink helps your stomach and intestines do their job?
cards.note: Water helps break food down and keeps everything moving. Drink some with every meal.
